title: Front Disc Brake Service (Post-1977 CJ-7)

parts.name: Centric front brake rotor (1978.5-1986 CJ-7 Dana 30)
Crown semi-metallic front pad set (1978-1981 two-bolt caliper)
Crown semi-metallic front pad set (1982-1986 with titanium dust shield)
Raybestos caliper guide pin and bushing kit

citations.title: Torque King QU80301 rotor — 1978.5-1985 CJ-7 Dana 30 spec

summary: Front disc brakes became standard on the CJ-7 in 1977. The Dana 30 with disc brakes uses a 10.5 in. rotor on a 5x5.5 bolt pattern, and the procedure is the same as any other vintage 4x4 disc swap — pads in 90 minutes, full rotor service in 3 hours.
description:
There are two distinct caliper generations to know about. 1976–1978 CJs used a six-bolt caliper bracket that bolts between the steering knuckle and the spindle. 1978.5–1986 went to a two-bolt caliper mount where the caliper bracket bolts directly to the knuckle. Year cutoff matters: order parts by VIN, not just by model year, because the changeover was mid-1978.

Pads on the 1978–1981 trucks use a two-bolt caliper plate. 1982–1986 CJ-7s added a titanium dust shield behind the pad — same caliper, different pad backing plate. Crown Automotive part numbers reflect both versions; cross-check before you order.

Rotors on the Dana 30 are inexpensive ($55–80 in semi-metallic). Resurfacing an old rotor is rarely worth the labor cost. If the rotor has lip wear deeper than the thickness of a quarter, it's past minimum spec — replace it. Minimum thickness is stamped on the rotor hat; if you can't read it, measure with calipers and compare to the new rotor.

The caliper itself is a single-piston floating design. Sticking guide pins are the most common cause of uneven pad wear and pulling. When the caliper is off, slide the guide pins out and inspect: the rubber bushings should be supple, not cracked. The Raybestos H5004 kit replaces both pins and bushings for under $20 and prevents a return trip in six months.

If the caliper piston is seized, replace the caliper outright. A rebuild kit is cheaper, but a 40-year-old caliper body often has pitting that defeats a new seal. Loaded calipers from Centric or Raybestos run $60–100 each.

**Safety pillar applies here.** Test the pedal before the first drive. Pump until firm. Drive 50 feet, brake gently. Then drive 200 feet, brake harder. If the pedal feels spongy, you have air in the line — bleed before you leave the driveway.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts a half-turn. Jack the front of the Jeep and set jack stands under the frame. Pull the wheels.
Spray the back of the caliper with brake parts cleaner to knock loose any debris that could spray when you crack fittings.
Pull the two caliper slide bolts (15mm on most years). Slide the caliper off the rotor. Hang it from the spring or coil with a wire — do not let it dangle from the brake hose.
Pry the old pads out of the bracket. Note their position; the outer pad has a wear sensor clip on some years.
Inspect the slide pins. If gritty or dry, pull them, clean them, and re-grease with high-temp brake caliper grease (or replace with the Raybestos kit).
Pull the rotor straight off the studs. If rust-locked, hit it with penetrant, wait 10 minutes, then strike the rotor face (not the hub) with a deadblow hammer.
Wire-brush the hub face clean. A rusty hub face is the #1 cause of brake pulsation on a fresh install.
Install the new rotor. Hand-thread two lug nuts to hold it flat against the hub.

Compress the caliper piston with a C-clamp or piston compressor. Open the bleeder on the caliper as you compress — pushing dirty fluid back up the line into the master cylinder is bad practice. Catch fluid in a rag.
Drop the new pads into the bracket. Reinstall the caliper over the new rotor. Torque caliper slide bolts to 25–35 ft-lb.
Wheels back on. Lug nut torque: 80 ft-lb on a 5x5.5 pattern.
Pump the brake pedal until firm before driving. Top off the master cylinder reservoir.
Bed the pads: 5 stops from 30 mph to 5 mph with moderate pressure, then 3 stops from 50 to 10 mph with firmer pressure. Don't lock the wheels.
pros: Massive safety improvement over neglected brakes — the single highest-leverage maintenance you can do
All parts are available, cheap, and shipping fast — no need to wait
Doable in an afternoon with hand tools
cons: Year cutoff at mid-1978 is real — confirm caliper type by VIN, not model year
If you have to push fluid back into the master cylinder, contamination risk goes up; open the bleeder while compressing
Old hardware (slide pins, clips, dust boots) is usually past its service life — budget for the full hardware kit, not just pads

title: Coolant Flush — AMC Sixes and V8s
summary: Both AMC engines in the CJ-7 hold around 11 quarts (258) to 14 quarts (304) of coolant total — and the radiator drain only pulls about half of that. To do a real flush, you have to drain the engine block too.
description:
The mistake most owners make is opening the radiator petcock, letting two gallons run out, refilling, and calling it done. The radiator on a CJ holds maybe 5 quarts. The rest sits in the engine block, the heater core, and the hoses. If you only drain the radiator, you're diluting old coolant with new — not flushing.

A real flush means opening the block drains on both sides of the engine (under the exhaust manifolds, easy to miss) or pulling the lower radiator hose. With the block open, you can run a garden hose into the radiator filler neck and watch the rusty water come out the bottom until it runs clear. Then you close everything up and refill with 50/50 distilled water and concentrated antifreeze.

Coolant chemistry on these engines is forgiving. Stock spec was green ethylene glycol. Universal "compatible with any color" formulations (Prestone AF2100, Peak Long Life) are fine. Avoid mixing Dex-Cool (orange, GM) with green in the same system — the byproducts can clog the heater core. If you're not sure what's in there, drain everything and start with one type.

Thermostat: stock is 195°F. If your engine runs hot in summer Phoenix-style heat, a 180°F thermostat (Stant 13558) buys 15°F of headroom — but a thermostat doesn't fix a clogged radiator or a worn water pump. Diagnose the cause first.

Distilled water matters. Tap water leaves mineral deposits in the radiator core that build up over years. If you're spending $40 on antifreeze, spend $4 on distilled water — don't undo the work.
steps: Engine cold. If the radiator is even warm to the touch, wait. Pressurized coolant against your face is the worst kind of preventable injury.
Place the drain pan under the radiator. Locate the petcock — driver-side bottom of the radiator on most CJ-7s.
Remove the radiator cap (cold engine only). Open the petcock counterclockwise. Let the radiator drain fully — about 5 quarts.

Locate the block drain plugs. On the AMC 258 they're on the driver side of the block, below the exhaust manifold (one plug, often a 3/8 in. square head). On the AMC 304 there are two — one each side. Use a wrench, not pliers; the heads round off easily.
Open each block drain. Catch the coolant. Plan on another 5–6 quarts coming out of the block.

If the coolant is brown/rusty: close the block drains, close the petcock, fill the radiator with distilled water only, run the engine to operating temp (heater on full hot), shut down, let cool, drain again. Repeat until water runs clear.
Pull the lower radiator hose for a final rinse if you want to be thorough — that's the only way to see actual flow direction.
Close all drains and reinstall the lower hose with fresh clamps.
Refill: 50% antifreeze concentrate, 50% distilled water, until the radiator is full and the overflow bottle reads "cold."
Start the engine with the cap off. Let it idle until the thermostat opens — you'll see the coolant level drop as air burps out. Top off the radiator. Replace the cap.
Drive 15 minutes. Let cool. Top off the overflow bottle to the cold line.
Recheck after one week of driving.
pros: Cheapest preventive maintenance against radiator and heater core failure
3-year / 50,000-mile interval is the standard; sooner if towing or seeing high desert temps
A clean cooling system runs 10–15°F cooler than a 5-year-old neglected one
cons: Block drain plugs are often seized or hidden behind exhaust manifolds — budget extra time for a first-time flush
Used coolant is toxic to pets; capture all of it and recycle at any auto parts store
A flush won't fix a clogged radiator, a worn water pump, or a failing thermostat — diagnose, then flush

title: Differential Fluid — Dana 30 Front, AMC 20 Rear
tools_required: 3/8 in. ratchet (square drive into fill plug)
fluid pump or gear oil squeeze bottle
RTV gasket sealant (if dropping the cover)

parts.name: Valvoline SynPower 80W-90 GL-5 gear oil (1 qt) — open diff
Royal Purple Max-Gear 75W-90 (1 qt) — limited-slip safe
Mopar friction modifier (for Trac-Lok limited slip)
Permatex Ultra Black RTV (if pulling the cover)

summary: The Dana 30 front takes 1.25 quarts of 80W-90 GL-5. The AMC 20 rear takes 2.4 quarts of the same. Both have a fill plug and a drain plug — no cover to drop unless you want to inspect the gears or run a full clean.
description:
This is the maintenance item that gets skipped longest because nothing visible signals that the fluid is dead. By the time the diff is whining, the gear faces are already pitted. The standard service interval is every 30,000 miles for daily-driver use, every 12,000 miles if you wheel hard, and immediately after any water crossing deep enough to submerge the diff cover. Water in gear oil turns it the color of coffee with cream — if you see that on the dipstick or fill-plug threads, change it now.

Both axles use the same 80W-90 GL-5 gear oil for open-diff applications. If your CJ-7 has the Trac-Lok limited-slip option in the rear, you also need a friction modifier — without it, the clutch packs will chatter on tight turns. Mopar friction modifier is the factory spec; one bottle treats one diff. Synthetic 80W-90 (Valvoline SynPower, Mobil 1 75W-90) is a worthwhile upgrade — better cold-weather pumping and slower oxidation.

Drain and fill plugs on the Dana 30 are both 3/8 in. square drive — you put the ratchet end directly into the plug, no socket needed. The fill plug is on the front face of the diff (between the pinion and the cover); the drain plug is below it. Old plugs can be tight. If you can't break the fill plug loose first, don't drain — you'll be stranded with an empty axle and no way to refill.

The AMC 20 rear uses the same 3/8 in. square drive on the fill plug. It's the differential many owners love to upgrade — the two-piece rear axle shaft is the well-known weak point, but the ring gear and diff itself are stout. Fluid change is the same procedure as the Dana 30, just more volume.

**The "loosen the fill plug first" rule is absolute.** Crack the fill plug before the drain plug, every time. Same logic as oil pan plug + filter — if the fill won't open, the drain stays closed.
steps: Drive the Jeep for 5 minutes to warm the gear oil. Warm oil drains faster and carries more contamination.
Park on level ground. Chock the rear wheels. Set the parking brake.
Wire-brush both plugs on the diff you're servicing — debris in the threads becomes debris in the diff.
Break the fill plug loose first. If it won't move with a 3/8 in. ratchet, hit it with penetrant, wait 10 minutes, try again. If it still won't move, do not drain.
Once the fill plug is loose, place the drain pan under the drain plug. Pull the drain plug. Let the gear oil drain fully — about 10 minutes.
Inspect the drained fluid. Metal sparkle from break-in (on a new gear set) is normal. Larger chunks or a milky color are not — diagnose before refilling.
Reinstall the drain plug. Torque to 24 ft-lb.
Pump fresh gear oil through the fill hole until it just starts to overflow back out — that's the correct level on any "fill to the hole" axle. Dana 30: ~1.25 qt. AMC 20: ~2.4 qt.
If running a Trac-Lok limited slip in the rear, add 4 oz of Mopar friction modifier (or equivalent) before the final fill.
Reinstall the fill plug. Torque to 24 ft-lb.
Wipe the diff clean. Drive a few miles and check for weep from either plug.
pros: Cheapest preventive maintenance against a $1,500+ ring-and-pinion replacement
Plug-and-fill design — no cover gasket, no RTV, no overnight cure time
Same fluid for both axles simplifies the parts list
cons: Old plugs can be seized — crack the fill before the drain or you'll regret it
If you crossed water and the fluid is milky, you need to pull the cover and inspect, not just refill
Trac-Lok diffs require friction modifier; missing this step makes the diff chatter in turns

title: Oil Change — AMC 258 I6 and AMC 304 V8
tools_required: oil filter wrench (3 3/8 in. cap or band)

parts.name: Shell Rotella T4 15W-40 (high-ZDDP for flat-tappet cam)

citations.title: AMC 304 oil capacity and weight discussion

summary: Both AMC engines in the CJ-7 take five quarts of 10W-30 or 15W-40, and both want a high-zinc (ZDDP) oil because the cam and lifters are flat-tappet — modern passenger car oils don't carry enough zinc to protect them.
description:
The 258 inline-six and the 304 V8 share the same service approach. Drain pan under the pan, pull the drain plug, swap the filter, refill with five quarts. Where DIYers get into trouble is oil selection, not procedure: modern API SP oils have ZDDP capped at ~800 ppm to protect catalytic converters in newer engines. That cap is fine for a roller-cam motor and a problem for a flat-tappet AMC. Cam wipe is the failure mode — and it shows up as a flat lobe a season later, not the day you change the oil.

The fix is to run a high-ZDDP oil. Diesel-rated 15W-40 (Shell Rotella T4) is the cheap path and still carries ~1,200 ppm zinc. Valvoline VR1 Racing 10W-30 carries more (~1,400 ppm) and costs more. Either is correct. Avoid generic "high-mileage" oils — they're high in detergent, not zinc.

Filter sizing matters on the 258 specifically. The long-bodied Wix 51258 sits close to the driver-side engine mount. If the mounts are soft (and on a 40-year-old Jeep they often are), high drivetrain torque can let the engine flex enough to tag the filter. Inspect the mounts before you commit to a long filter. If they look cooked, install fresh mounts or run the shorter Wix 51522 — same threading, shorter can, more clearance.

The 304 V8 takes the Wix 51515 — a different filter entirely. Don't cross them.

Total capacity for both engines with a new filter is five quarts. Some shops recommend 5.5 quarts ("five plus a half for the filter") which lands the dipstick a hair above the full mark — fine, but the official spec is five.
steps: Run the engine for 5 minutes to warm the oil and suspend the sludge.
Park on level ground with the front wheels chocked. Set the parking brake.
Slide the drain pan under the pan plug (passenger-side rear corner on the 258, sump bottom on the 304).
Pull the 13mm or 1/2 in. drain plug. Let it drain for at least 10 minutes — drips matter.
Position the pan under the filter (driver-side block, mid-engine). Spin the filter off with a cap or band wrench.
Wipe the filter mounting surface clean. Pre-fill the new filter with fresh oil. Smear oil on the new gasket.
Thread the new filter on by hand. When the gasket touches the block, snug it 3/4 turn — no wrench.
Reinstall the drain plug with the crush washer (replace if flattened). Torque: 25 ft-lb on both engines.
Add five quarts of high-ZDDP oil. Start the engine. Watch for the oil pressure light to drop within 5 seconds.
Check for leaks at the filter and drain plug. Shut down. Recheck the dipstick after 5 minutes of settling.
pros: Cheapest and highest-leverage maintenance on either AMC engine
Done in 30 minutes once you have the routine
Keeps the flat-tappet cam alive — every change matters
cons: Filter clearance to the driver-side motor mount on the 258 is tight; soft mounts compound the problem
ZDDP requirement narrows your oil shelf at most parts stores — diesel section or specialty racing oils only

title: Spark Plugs — AMC 258 and 304
tools_required: spark plug gap tool or feeler gauge
summary: Both the AMC 258 and 304 use Champion RN12YC (or equivalent) at 0.035 in. gap and 26–30 ft-lb torque into cast iron heads. Anti-seize is optional but recommended on a 40-year-old aluminum-free engine that has seen seasonal humidity.
description:
This is the second-cheapest tune-up you can do, and the one that most often gets skipped because the engine "still runs." The 258 will tolerate worn plugs for tens of thousands of miles before it stumbles. By the time it stumbles, the cap, rotor, and wires are probably also tired. Fresh plugs every 20,000 miles on a daily-driver CJ-7 is the standard interval; every 5,000 if it sees serious dust or short trips.

The 258 firing order is **1-5-3-6-2-4** (front to back: cylinders 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). The 304 V8 is **1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2** — passenger bank is 1, 3, 5, 7 front to back; driver bank is 2, 4, 6, 8 front to back. Pull and label one wire at a time so you don't have to relearn the order. If wires are cracked, ceramic insulators are oil-stained, or the boots feel hard, replace the whole set. NAPA Belden or Accel 5mm wires are the standard upgrade.

Stock plug for both engines is the Champion RN12YC copper. The "RN" prefix means resistor, nominal heat range; the "12Y" is the heat number; the "C" denotes copper core. NGK BPR5ES is the direct cross-reference and many owners prefer it for a sharper spark in worn engines. Avoid platinum or iridium plugs unless your ignition is upgraded — the stock points-or-Motorcraft ignition doesn't put out the voltage to clean a fine-tip plug.

Gap is **0.035 in.** on both engines. The factory tolerance is 0.033–0.038 in. The 258 with HEI distributor (1978+ on most Jeeps) can run 0.040 in. if the coil is healthy, but stay at 0.035 if you've got original ignition.
steps: Let the engine cool completely. Aluminum-thread strip is not the concern (these heads are cast iron) but a hot plug can seize against carbon.
Blow or brush debris out of each plug well before you crack any plug loose. Dirt that falls into the cylinder doesn't come back out.
Pull one plug wire by the boot — never the wire itself. Twist a quarter-turn first to break the boot seal.
Loosen and remove the plug with a 5/8 in. plug socket and 6 in. extension. Inspect the old plug: tan tip is healthy, black sooty tip is rich running, white tip is lean or overheated.
Set the gap on the new plug to **0.035 in.** with a feeler or wire gauge. Confirm — every new plug ships from the factory pre-gapped to something, and "pre-gapped" doesn't mean "right."
Apply a thin smear of anti-seize to the plug threads only (not the electrode). Hand-thread the plug fully — if it doesn't spin in by hand, stop and check the threads.
Torque to **26–30 ft-lb** on cast iron heads.
Reattach the plug wire. Push the boot on until you feel and hear it click on the terminal.
Repeat one cylinder at a time. Doing it one-at-a-time prevents wire-crossing.
Start the engine. It should fire cleanly. A rough idle that smooths out in 30 seconds is normal — the new plugs are burning off oil residue.
pros: Catches developing problems (oil-fouled plug = ring or valve seal issue; carbon-bridged plug = idle running too cool)
30-minute job once you have the rhythm
cons: Easy to cross-thread on a head that's seen decades of heat cycles — go slow and hand-thread every plug
Wire crossover (firing order wrong) is the #1 failure mode for first-time CJ owners; pull one at a time
